introduction.p: The conclusions of Rolle's Theorem, the Mean Value Theorem, derivative tests for extrema, and l'Hospital's Rule depend on their hypotheses. The examples below show failures caused by missing continuity, differentiability, endpoint conditions, or sign conditions.

subsection.p: There is no contradiction. Fermat’s theorem applies to interior points. At an endpoint, the graph only has to be compared with points on one side. It can be best or worst without flattening out.

subsection.p: That is why the closed interval method always checks endpoints separately.

exercise.title: Why can an endpoint extremum fail to have a horizontal tangent?

statement.p: On [0,1], the function f(x)=x attains its max and min, but f' is never zero. In your own words, why is that compatible with Fermat’s theorem, and why does the closed interval method therefore check endpoints separately?

hint.p: Fermat’s theorem applies to interior points. At an endpoint the graph is compared with only one side, so it can be best or worst without flattening.

exercise.title: Why can the Mean Value Theorem fail without continuity or differentiability?

statement.p: A jump on the closed interval, or a corner inside, can keep every existing tangent slope away from the secant slope. In your own words, why are continuity on [a,b] and differentiability on (a,b) not decorations, and what kind of escape does each hypothesis block?

hint.p: Continuity keeps the graph from leaping over the needed height. Differentiability keeps a turn from happening at a corner instead of at a tangent.

paragraphs.title: A derivative quotient with no limit
paragraphs.p: Sometimes the original quotient has a limit, but the quotient of derivatives does not.

There is no contradiction. l’Hospital’s Rule says that if the original quotient has the right indeterminate form and the derivative quotient has a limit, then the original limit has that same value. It does not say that the derivative quotient must always have a limit.

p.em: If the derivative quotient does not settle, l'Hospital's Rule gives no conclusion.

exercise.title: Why is l’Hospital’s Rule not a license for every quotient?

statement.p: The rule applies only to certain indeterminate quotients, and only when the derivative quotient has a limit. In your own words, why can blindly differentiating a well-behaved quotient give the wrong answer, and why can a derivative quotient that refuses to settle leave the original limit still well-defined?

hint.p: A theorem is a package: hypotheses imply a conclusion. Missing hypotheses mean the theorem is no longer the reason, even if luck later produces a true statement.

subsection.title: A theorem-use checklist
subsection.p: The warnings can be compressed into a practical checklist.

cell.p: Is the extremum at an interior point? Is the function differentiable there?
Is the function continuous on [a,b]? Is it differentiable on (a,b)?
Does f' actually change sign around the critical number?
Is f'(c)=0? Is f''(c) positive or negative, not zero?
Is the quotient really 0/0 or \infty/\infty? Does the derivative quotient have a limit?

subsection.p: A theorem is not only a conclusion. It is a package:
If the hypotheses are missing, the conclusion may still be true by luck. But the theorem is no longer the reason.

These warnings prepare the chapter review. We now gather the ideas into one working map: how to read shape from derivatives, how to prove global facts from the Mean Value Theorem, and how to tell when a tempting shortcut is legal.
